title: Huffman Encoding
directAnswer: Build an optimal prefix code by repeatedly merging the two LEAST frequent symbols into a parent whose frequency is their sum, using a min-heap. Each merge creates an internal tree node; after n−1 merges one root remains. A symbol's code length equals its depth in this tree, so rare symbols sit deep (long codes) and frequent symbols sit shallow (short codes). The total encoded bits = Σ frequency × depth, and this greedy provably minimises it. O(n log n) with a min-heap.

remember.pattern: Min-heap: merge the two lowest-frequency nodes until one tree remains
remember.formula:
heap = min-heap of leaf nodes (by frequency)
while heap size > 1:
    a = pop min
    b = pop min
    parent = node(freq = a.freq + b.freq, left = a, right = b)
    push parent
root = pop
# code length of a symbol = its depth; assign 0/1 down each edge
rules: Always merge the **two smallest-frequency** nodes — the same two-smallest greedy as connecting ropes.
The merged node's frequency is the **sum** of its children; push it back so it competes in future merges.
It's a **prefix code**: every symbol is a leaf, so no code is a prefix of another and decoding is unambiguous.
A symbol's **code length = its depth** in the tree, so total bits = Σ freq × depth — exactly the merge-cost sum.
Multiple optimal trees can exist (ties break differently), but the total encoded length is unique.
whenToUse: Build a variable-length prefix code that minimises total encoded length
Compress data where symbol frequencies are known and skewed
Any 'merge two cheapest, cost = sum, minimise total' optimal-binary-merge-tree problem
You need an unambiguous code where no codeword prefixes another
antiSignals: All symbols equally frequent → fixed-length codes are already optimal, Huffman gives no gain
You need codes of bounded maximum length → length-limited Huffman (package-merge), not plain greedy
Frequencies arrive as a stream / change over time → adaptive Huffman or arithmetic coding
You want the best possible ratio, not just prefix-optimal → arithmetic / range coding beats Huffman
remember.takeaway: Huffman is the canonical optimal prefix code: merge the two rarest symbols repeatedly so rare symbols end up deep (long codes) and common ones shallow (short codes). It's the same min-heap merge as 'connect ropes', and the exchange argument — the two lowest-frequency symbols can always be made deepest siblings — is what proves it optimal.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you build the tree bottom-up by always merging the two lowest-frequency nodes with a min-heap, understand that code length equals tree depth, and can argue why greedy yields a minimum-total-length prefix code.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Merging the two largest, forgetting to push the merged node back so it can be re-merged, or assigning codes to internal nodes instead of only leaves (breaking the prefix property).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the exchange argument — the two least frequent symbols can be assumed to be the deepest siblings in some optimal tree, so merging them first is safe — and connect it to the optimal-binary-merge-tree family (connect ropes, file merging).

problemStatement:
You are given `n` symbols, each with a non-negative `frequency` (how often it appears). Construct a binary **prefix code** — a binary tree whose leaves are the symbols — that minimises the total number of encoded bits, where a symbol contributes `frequency × (its depth in the tree)` bits.

Return the ***minimum total encoded length*** (and/or the code assigned to each symbol). A prefix code means no symbol's codeword is a prefix of another's, which is guaranteed when every symbol is a leaf.
constraints: Total encoded length can exceed 32 bits → accumulate in a long
For n = 1 the single symbol is conventionally given a code of length 1 (one bit)
understanding: Picture a binary tree whose leaves are the symbols. Walking from the root, each left/right edge appends a 0/1 bit, so a leaf's codeword is the path to it and its length is its depth. Because symbols are only at leaves, no codeword is a prefix of another — decoding is unambiguous. The total cost is Σ frequency × depth, and minimising it means keeping high-frequency symbols shallow. Greedily merging the two rarest nodes builds exactly that tree from the bottom up.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why must symbols be at the leaves only?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: To keep it a prefix code. If a symbol sat at an internal node, its codeword would be a prefix of every codeword below it, making decoding ambiguous. Leaves-only guarantees the prefix property.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the optimal tree unique?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not necessarily — ties in frequency can be broken differently, and left/right is arbitrary. But the minimum total encoded length is unique.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the code length for a single symbol?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: With one symbol there's no real tree; by convention it gets a 1-bit code, so the cost is its frequency × 1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the total bit count overflow 32 bits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: With 10⁵ symbols at 10⁹ frequency and non-trivial depths, the sum easily exceeds int range. I accumulate it in a 64-bit long.

examples.explanation: Classic example. Merging the two smallest repeatedly gives f a 1-bit-ish shallow placement and a,b deep. Total bits Σ freq×depth = 224 (e.g. a=1100, b=1101, c=100, d=101, e=111, f=0).
Merge 2+3=5, 4+5=9, 6+9=15 → total of merge sums 5+9+15 = 29. Same arithmetic as connecting ropes.
A single symbol gets a 1-bit code by convention → 10 × 1 = 10.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. 'Optimal prefix code from frequencies' lands on the min-heap merge.

approaches.name: Repeated Two-Smallest Merge (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this to fix the greedy idea — merge the two rarest symbols — and the 'code length = depth' insight before swapping the slow lookup for a heap.
hints: A symbol's code length is its depth in the tree, so total bits = Σ frequency × depth. To shrink the total, which symbols should sit deepest (longest codes)?
The rarest ones. So build the tree bottom-up: repeatedly take the two lowest-frequency nodes and join them under a new parent whose frequency is their sum.

Without a heap: each round scan all live nodes for the two smallest frequencies, merge them, and add the new parent back. Repeat until one node remains; the answer is the sum of all merge frequencies.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each round scans up to n live nodes for the two smallest → O(n) per round, with n−1 merges → O(n²). Storing nodes costs O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Treat each symbol as a leaf node carrying its frequency. Each round, find the two nodes with the lowest frequencies, create a parent whose frequency is their sum (with those two as children), and add the parent back to the pool. After `n − 1` merges a single root remains; the minimum total encoded length is the sum of all the parent frequencies created along the way.

**Why total bits equals Σ frequency × depth.** Each left/right edge from the root adds one bit to a codeword, so a leaf at depth `d` has a `d`-bit code and contributes `frequency × d` bits. Equivalently, every time a node is buried under a new parent its frequency is counted one more time — which is exactly why summing the parent frequencies over all merges equals `Σ frequency × depth`. That dual view (sum of merge costs = weighted depth) is the same identity as connecting ropes.

**Why merge the two rarest.** You want long codes (deep leaves) for symbols that appear rarely, since their length is multiplied by a small frequency. Merging the two lowest-frequency nodes pushes them one level deeper and creates a combined node that, being small, will likely be merged again soon — keeping rare symbols sinking while frequent symbols stay near the root. That's the greedy that minimises the weighted depth.

**Why prefix-correctness is automatic.** Because symbols only ever become leaves (we merge nodes into a *new* parent, never attach a symbol mid-tree), no codeword is a prefix of another. The tree structure itself enforces the prefix property.

**Why we don't ship this.** Re-scanning all live nodes for the two minimums every round is `O(n²)`. We only ever need the two smallest repeatedly, with one insertion after each merge — the textbook case for a min-heap, which the optimal approach uses.
approaches.insight: The algorithm is one greedy rule — merge the two rarest — justified by 'code length = depth'. The O(n²) is purely the repeated scan for the two minimums; a min-heap finds them in O(log n) and is the only change needed.

dryRun.intro: Each round merge the two lowest-frequency nodes; the new parent frequency is their sum. Total = Σ parent frequencies.

code.python:
def huffman_cost(self, freq: list[int]) -> int:
    if len(freq) == 1:
        return freq[0]                 # single symbol: 1-bit code
    pool = list(freq)
    total = 0
    while len(pool) > 1:
        pool.sort()                    # O(n log n) per round on purpose: the slow baseline
        a = pool.pop(0)
        b = pool.pop(0)
        total += a + b
        pool.append(a + b)
    return total

Scan for the lowest-frequency node — O(n).
Parent frequency = sum of the two rarest children.
Adding every parent frequency yields Σ freq × depth, the total encoded bits.

python.explanation: Single-symbol convention: cost is its frequency × 1 bit.
Re-sorting each round to expose the two smallest is what makes this baseline slow.
The merged parent re-enters the pool to compete in later merges.

edgeCases.behavior: One merge, both at depth 1 → total = freq[0] + freq[1].

pitfalls: Merging the two LARGEST — gives rare symbols short codes, maximising total bits.
Assigning codes to internal nodes — breaks the prefix property.
Skipping this approach — verbalising 'merge the two rarest, code length = depth' is what the interviewer grades.

approaches.name: Min-Heap Tree Construction (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'I only need the two smallest repeatedly, so a min-heap builds the tree in O(n log n)'.
hints: You never need all nodes sorted — only the two smallest, repeatedly, with one push after each merge. Which structure gives min-removal and insertion in O(log n)?
Build a min-heap of nodes keyed by frequency. Pop the two smallest, make a parent with their summed frequency, push the parent back.
Repeat until one node (the root) remains. Accumulate each parent's frequency for the total bits; to emit codes, walk the tree assigning 0 going left and 1 going right.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Heapify is O(n). There are n−1 merges; each does two pops and one push, all O(log n) → O(n log n). The heap and tree hold O(n) nodes → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Put every symbol into a min-heap keyed by frequency. While more than one node remains, pop the two smallest, create a parent whose frequency is their sum (children = the two popped nodes), and push the parent back. The last remaining node is the root. The minimum total encoded length is the sum of all parent frequencies; the per-symbol codes come from a traversal that appends `0` on each left edge and `1` on each right edge.

**Why a min-heap is the right structure.** The baseline only ever needs: remove the smallest, remove the next smallest, insert the merged parent. A min-heap does each in `O(log n)`, so the whole construction is `O(n log n)` — versus the baseline's `O(n²)` re-scan.

**The exchange argument that proves optimality.** Let the two least-frequent symbols be `x` and `y`. Claim: some optimal tree has `x` and `y` as sibling leaves at maximum depth. Take any optimal tree and let `a` and `b` be two deepest sibling leaves. Since `x` and `y` are the least frequent, swapping `x` with `a` and `y` with `b` never increases `Σ freq × depth` (moving a smaller frequency deeper and a larger one shallower can only help or tie). So there's an optimal tree where `x` and `y` are deepest siblings. Replacing that pair with a single merged leaf of frequency `freq(x)+freq(y)` reduces the problem to `n − 1` symbols, and the cost differs by exactly `freq(x)+freq(y)` — the merge cost we add. Inductively, the greedy that merges the two smallest each step is optimal.

**Why summing parent frequencies gives the answer.** Each merge's parent frequency is counted again in every later merge it participates in — that compounding is precisely `Σ freq × depth`. Accumulating `a.freq + b.freq` on every merge captures the total encoded length without ever computing depths explicitly.

**Why decoding is unambiguous.** Symbols are only ever leaves, so no codeword prefixes another. A decoder walks the tree bit by bit from the root and emits a symbol exactly when it reaches a leaf.

**Practical notes.** Keep frequencies and the total in 64-bit (`long` in Java; Python ints are unbounded). Decide a deterministic tie-break (e.g. insertion order) if you need reproducible codes, since equal frequencies can yield different but equally optimal trees.
approaches.insight: This is the same optimal-binary-merge-tree engine as connecting ropes, but the tree is the deliverable: depths become code lengths. Whenever a baseline repeatedly needs 'the two smallest, then reinsert', a min-heap is the upgrade, and the exchange argument is the standard way to prove the greedy optimal.

dryRun.intro: Min-heap of frequencies. Merge two smallest each step; parent freq = sum. Total = Σ parent freqs.

code.python:
import heapq

def huffman_cost(self, freq: list[int]) -> int:
    if len(freq) == 1:
        return freq[0]
    # heap entries: (frequency, tie_breaker, node) — tie_breaker keeps it comparable
    heap = [[f, i, None] for i, f in enumerate(freq)]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    counter = len(freq)
    total = 0
    while len(heap) > 1:
        a = heapq.heappop(heap)
        b = heapq.heappop(heap)
        merged_freq = a[0] + b[0]
        total += merged_freq
        heapq.heappush(heap, [merged_freq, counter, (a, b)])
        counter += 1
    return total

java.line: PriorityQueue<Node> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Long.compare(x.freq, y.freq));
java.explanation: Min-heap ordered by frequency — always hands back the two rarest nodes.

java.line: Node parent = new Node(a.freq + b.freq, a, b);
java.explanation: New internal node; the two rarest become its children, sinking one level deeper.
Summed parent frequencies equal Σ freq × depth — the total encoded bits.

java.line: return total; // heap.peek() is the root of the code tree
java.explanation: The lone remaining node is the root; traverse it to emit per-symbol codes.

python.line: heap = [[f, i, None] for i, f in enumerate(freq)]
python.explanation: The index i is a tie-breaker so heapq never has to compare the node payloads.
Parent frequency = sum of the two rarest. Python ints can't overflow, so no long needed.
Push the parent (carrying its children) back to compete in later merges.

edgeCases.behavior: Returned early with a 1-bit code; no merges happen.
Builds a balanced tree; every code has the same length — Huffman ties fixed-length coding.
The frequent symbol stays near the root (short code); rare symbols sink deep — maximum compression benefit.

pitfalls: Comparing node objects directly in Python's heapq without a tie-breaker — throws when frequencies tie.
Using a max-heap or merging the two largest — produces the worst, not best, total length.
Forgetting the n = 1 case — a lone symbol still needs a 1-bit code, not zero.

commonMistakes: Merging the two highest-frequency nodes instead of the two lowest.
Assigning codewords to internal nodes, which destroys the prefix property.
Forgetting to push the merged parent back, so it never participates in later merges.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Merging the two largest
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Code length is depth, and you want rare symbols deep. Merging the largest first gives frequent symbols long codes and rare ones short codes — the maximum total length, exact opposite of the goal.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: PriorityQueue<Node> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Long.compare(y.freq, x.freq)); // max-heap
commonMistakesDetailed.good: PriorityQueue<Node> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Long.compare(x.freq, y.freq)); // min-heap

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Uncomparable nodes in Python heapq
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Pushing (freq, node) tuples makes heapq compare node objects when two freqs tie, raising a TypeError. Add a unique increasing counter as a tie-breaker so comparison never reaches the payload.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: heapq.heappush(heap, (merged_freq, (a, b)))   # compares tuples → may compare a,b

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on total bits
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With 10⁵ symbols at 10⁹ frequency and non-trivial depths, Σ freq × depth exceeds 2³¹ and an int total wraps negative.

patternNote: Canonical optimal prefix code via the optimal-binary-merge-tree greedy. Recognise it whenever you minimise Σ frequency × depth (or any 'merge two cheapest, cost = sum, minimise total'): a min-heap merging the two smallest builds the tree in O(n log n). Same engine as connecting ropes; the exchange argument proves the two rarest can be deepest siblings.
